extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of Nature (scientists, researchers, authors, and publishers circa 1907)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of evaluative standards and procedural criteria appearing in a Nature issue: standards used to judge technical books and textbooks, principles for experimental method and replication, and the journal's correspondence/submission policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and correspondence policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by his correspondents, neither can he undertake to return, or to correspond with the writers of, rejected manuscripts. No notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy statement printed as heading to 'Letters to the Editor' section; indicates no authorial or editorial responsibility for views, no manuscript returns, no correspondence about rejected submissions, and refusal to consider anonymous submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and authority of technical books
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable technical book is 'filled from cover to cover with the practical remarks of a man who knows his subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praises works that provide practical, experience-based guidance useful to practitioners (manufacturers, designers, users). Presence of authorial practical insight is a mark of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenient arrangement and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The matter should be 'conveniently arranged' so readers can follow the development of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good organization aids comprehension across audiences; reviewer notes arrangement as a criterion for evaluating the book's usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and accessibility for intended readership
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader, whether manufacturer, designer, or user, must be 'able to follow the author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity of exposition and suitability of level for intended audiences (practitioners vs. theorists) is important; the book should enable practical application or understanding by its target readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of controversial points and explicit opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should state 'very decided opinions on many of the controversial points which have arisen during the development' of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong work gives clear positions on debated issues, enabling readers to assess arguments; however such dicta should remain open to challenge if erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and coverage of important topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters devoted to details are 'very complete; every important organ is considered and discussed separately.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive coverage of essential subtopics and components, discussed in detail and separately, is a mark of a high-quality technical manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and clarity of drawings and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings should be 'real drawings and not process blocks,' and consequently 'far clearer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical illustrations must be accurate, clear, and well-executed; poor reproduction methods that obscure detail detract from a work's usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness and novelty of compiled empirical data (tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of 'tables of the principal dimensions of the best known cars of the day' accompanied by 'very full notes'—a valuable compilation and 'the first time that anyone has attempted to collect together such a mass of useful information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing together empirical data and reference tables with explanatory notes adds exceptional practical value; novelty in data compilation is specifically commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and readiness to point out errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer notes a 'peculiar error' on a specific page and says 'a few other dicta laid down by the author may be challenged,' implying accuracy is a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work should be factually accurate; reviewers will call out errors and judge the work accordingly. Isolated mistakes reduce authority and should be assessed in context of overall value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall utility to practitioners (necessity for library)
rubrics_metrics.description: A book that contains valuable tables, data, and carefully reasoned conclusions is 'almost a necessity for everyone who is closely interested in the modern motor-car to keep this book in his library.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final evaluative judgment includes whether the work is essential or highly useful to practitioners and specialists in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical content for textbooks: experiments and worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks should include 'easy experiments inserted throughout the book,' numerous diagrams, and a 'variety and number of Examples to be worked out by the student; there are 40 Test Papers and Miscellaneous Examples containing problems of a practical type.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For instructional texts, the number and quality of exercises, presence of experimental demonstrations, and variety of problems are central to pedagogical effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edition options: provision of answers and modular parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are usefully 'issued in the following ways' — complete or in parts, 'with or without Answers' — allowing choice for self-study or examination uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering editions with/without answers or modular parts (Part I, Part II) is a publication practice that affects usability for teachers, students, and self-learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption by reputable schools and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A textbook's quality is signalled by being 'in use at Harrow, Rugby, ... Oxford, ... Melbourne, Sydney, New Zealand, South Africa, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread adoption by recognized schools and colleges is used as evidence of suitability and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of purpose and stated aim of a work
rubrics_metrics.description: A booklet can be criticized if reviewers are 'at a loss to discover object and aim'—lack of clear aim undermines usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books and pamphlets should clearly state their objective and intended contribution; vague or indistinct purpose weakens critical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method appropriateness (design and technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regnault's method had shortcomings: temperature observed depended on the position of the thermometer; experimental method 'was not in this case the best that might have been devised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments must use appropriate methods and apparatus placement; sensitivity of results to measurement setup signals methodological problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument reliability and acknowledgement of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Results may be impaired by 'imperfect electrical instruments of the time'; the fault in thermoelectric measurements was probably with the instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should assess instrument limitations and uncertainty; recognition of instrument-induced error is a part of rigorous experimental reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete reporting of experimental conditions and statistical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Regnault 'does not state the temperature at which his experiments were made,' but reports means and ranges (e.g., mean of eleven measurements, extreme values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate reporting of experimental conditions (temperature, pressure, apparatus dimensions) and of statistical summaries (means, ranges, number of measurements) is required for reproducibility and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison and consistency with prior studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental results should be compared with contemporaneous work (comparison of Regnault's mean At/Ap with Joule and Kelvin's results shows 'in reality his work agreed fairly well').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situating new measurements in context of established results helps evaluate validity and identify systematic discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between observing a phenomenon and testing its interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating Mendel's experiments (observing the phenomenon) is not equivalent to 'repeating... with the deliberate intention of testing the Mendelian interpretation' (testing the inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific rigor requires experiments specifically designed to discriminate between competing interpretations, not merely to reproduce observed outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing crucial, decisive experiments (falsification-oriented)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested crucial experiment: cross a pure yellow with an 'extracted green' (a green whose ancestry is overwhelmingly yellow) to see if Mendelian proportions hold — such a result would be decisive for the interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments aimed at falsifying or decisively testing hypotheses should be constructed so that outcomes leave no reasonable doubt about the validity of the interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical replication by independent observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Crucial experiments should be 'carried out by one who is actively sceptical of Mendel's hypothesis' so the result can persuade a doubter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replications performed by skeptical, independent researchers strengthen the evidential force of experimental results and reduce bias in interpretation.
